findings.claim: `isDone` is only set to `true` in the `.then()` handler, never on rejection, so a failed request is still treated as in-flight by any teardown/abort logic guarded on `isDone`.
findings.rationale: The new `isDone` flag exists to tell the teardown whether the request already settled. Because there is no assignment in the promise's rejection path (or an equivalent `finally`), unsubscribing after a network/parse failure will take the `!isDone` branch and call `ac.abort()` on an already-settled operation. Likely harmless in the common case but can emit a stray AbortError and skews the batch's abort bookkeeping. Medium confidence, since the teardown code is not visible in this hunk.

findings.claim: `loader.load({...op, signal: ...})` passes a shallow clone instead of the original `op`, changing the operation object's identity for all downstream consumers.
findings.rationale: Previously the exact `op` reference reached the dataloader and the HTTP layer. Any code keying on operation identity (batch maps, WeakMap-based context, interceptors, or tests asserting the received operation) will no longer see the same object. It also means `op.signal` observed downstream is the derived race signal rather than the caller's signal. Moderate confidence that this is at least a behavior change worth verifying.

findings.claim: `raceAbortSignals` is used without a visible import, and its behavior with an `undefined` or already-aborted `op.signal` is unverified.
findings.rationale: `op.signal` is optional, so the first argument can be `undefined`; and if the caller's signal is already aborted before `load()` is called, the composed signal must be pre-aborted or an already-cancelled request will still be dispatched. Additionally, if the helper is not already imported in this file the change won't compile. Low-to-medium confidence because imports and the helper implementation are outside this hunk.

findings.claim: The per-operation `AbortController` is never aborted on the success path, so abort listeners registered on a long-lived `op.signal` are retained indefinitely.
findings.rationale: `raceAbortSignals` typically attaches an `abort` listener to each input signal. If the caller reuses one controller across many operations (common in component-scoped cancellation) and `ac` is never aborted after completion, listeners accumulate for the lifetime of that signal. This is a leak rather than a correctness bug; confidence is low because the helper may use `AbortSignal.any`, which is GC-friendly.
